title: One in Three Teachers Leave Within Five Years. Perhaps We're Asking the Wrong Question.
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes questions whether the standard explanations for teacher attrition - workload, pay, behaviour, accountability - miss a quieter factor: many early-career teachers leave because they are never given room to develop a coherent professional identity. Citing research on pre-service teachers' professional identity built from motivation, self-efficacy, responsibility, commitment and perceived expertise, she argues identity is fluid and requires space to be tested through experimentation and reflection, not simply delivered through observation checklists. She warns that when evidence-informed teaching becomes evidence-enforced compliance, mentoring drifts from developing judgement toward auditing performed behaviours, and novices begin confusing compliance with expertise. The piece closes by arguing that mentoring's real purpose is to help identity emerge, not to replace it with fidelity to a framework, and that this may be an overlooked piece of the retention puzzle.
points: Hughes's core claim is that attrition may be driven partly by identity starvation - early-career teachers never given room to discover who they are as professionals, not just workload or pay alone.
She distinguishes evidence-informed practice from evidence-enforced compliance, arguing the latter shifts novice teachers from asking what pupils need to asking what the observer wants to see.
Her citation of a teacher whose self-perception collapsed from 'competent' to 'competent in nothing' under classroom pressure illustrates how fragile unsupported identity construction can be.
She reframes mentoring's purpose as helping identity emerge through questions like 'why did you choose that approach?' rather than assessing fidelity to prescribed techniques.
quotes: What if many early career teachers leave because they are never given the opportunity to become the teacher they hoped they would be?

Confidence rose after lessons that felt successful and meaningful, only to fall after difficult classroom experiences. Commitment strengthened when mentoring relationships were supportive and expectations were clear, but weakened when participants encountered inconsistent guidance or overwhelming pressure.

The problem emerges when evidence-informed practice quietly becomes evidence-enforced compliance. Instead of asking, What do these pupils need right now?, novice teachers may find themselves wondering, What does my observer want to see?

One participant moved from identifying herself as competent to feeling competent in nothing after experiencing overwhelming classroom pressures. Her sense of professional identity was shaken not because she lacked intelligence or commitment, but because the emotional realities of teaching overwhelmed an identity that was still under construction.
Perhaps they are not leaving because they dislike teaching. Perhaps they are leaving because they were never given enough time, trust or space to become teachers in the fullest sense of the word.
